content_voiceover: Let's talk about chronic lymphocytic leukemia, or CLL. On flow cytometry, the classic immunophenotype is CD5 positive and CD23 positive, which distinguishes CLL from mantle cell lymphoma, since mantle cell is also CD5 positive but CD23 negative. CLL cells also show weak expression of surface immunoglobulin, CD79b, CD22, and cyclin D1, with negative FMC7, so overall a weak pan B cell marker pattern. Clinically, CLL can be complicated by autoimmune cytopenias like ITP or autoimmune hemolytic anemia, and patients may develop hypogammaglobulinemia predisposing them to infections. About three to four percent of cases undergo Richter transformation into a higher grade lymphoma, usually diffuse large B cell lymphoma. Epidemiologically, CLL is the most common leukemia in the Western world, but it's notably rare in Taiwan, at roughly one fifth the Western incidence, making up only one to three percent of non-Hodgkin lymphomas here. There's a male predominance of about two to one, and the median age at diagnosis is seventy two years old.
keypoints: CD5 positive, CD23 positive on flow cytometry
Richter transformation occurs in three to four percent
Most common leukemia in the West, rare in Taiwan
Median age at diagnosis is seventy two years
